children: By Robbie Whelan

U.S. negotiators used the promise of access to Nvidia's artificial-intelligence chips to help secure a preliminary peace deal reached last year between the nations of Armenia and Azerbaijan, according to people involved in the talks.

The inclusion of expanded approvals for chip purchases for an Armenian data-center project as an inducement for the country to participate, which hasn't been previously reported, represents one of the most striking instances to date of what U.S. officials are calling chip diplomacy.

While the Trump administration has also used AI hardware to negotiate agreements with the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, the Armenia deal is one of the first known instances of the administration using them to help clinch a peace deal, diplomats and experts say. The deal deepened ties between the White House and the world's largest chip designer, whose chief executive, Jensen Huang, speaks regularly with President Trump and advises him on AI policy.

Last month, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan gathered with regional leaders and executives from Nvidia, Dell and other companies for a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a massive data-center project in the city of Hrazdan, about 30 miles from the Azerbaijan border.

The project, known as Firebird, is expected to eventually cost upward of $5 billion to build. Its developers plan to pack it with 70,000 of Nvidia's latest AI servers, known as Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin, representing about 300 megawatts of computing power, by the end of next year.

At the ceremony, Prime Minister Pashinyan called the data center a "major achievement" and credited Trump with helping to make it happen by signing a memorandum of understanding last year that deepened Armenia's ties with the U.S. on tech and trade.

Much less has been said publicly about the role that Firebird played in getting a deal meant to end a decadeslong dispute between Armenia and Azerbaijan that had spilled over into armed conflict over the breakaway region of Nagorno-Karabakh. The territory was long held by ethnic Armenians inside the internationally recognized borders of Azerbaijan.

Last spring, about a year and a half after Azerbaijan regained control of the territory, fragile talks between Pashinyan and Azerbaijan's president, Ilham Aliyev, looked in danger of collapsing. Armenia, a mostly Christian nation, and majority-Muslim Azerbaijan have had intermittent clashes for more than 35 years, since before the collapse of the Soviet Union, of which both were member republics. Nearly 40,000 people have died in violence between the two countries, according to some estimates.

When the Trump administration took office in early 2025, it made peace in the South Caucasus a priority, sending diplomats to Yerevan, the Armenian capital, to help pressure leaders to hammer out an agreement.  The American negotiating team assessed that Pashinyan viewed the political cost of merely resolving the conflict as being too high, the U.S. diplomats said. They thought Armenia would be more likely to agree to a peace deal if the country was offered closer economic ties to the U.S.
That included authorizing more powerful Nvidia chips for sale in Armenia, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

A spokeswoman for Pashinyan said that establishing peace with Azerbaijan has been "the most important promise" of the prime minister's government and that he had a "clear mandate from the people" to do so. The bilateral agreements signed in Washington last August, "including the MOU on semiconductors and artificial intelligence, represent important peace dividends offered to Armenia," she said.
Hikmat Hajiyev, a spokesman for Azerbaijan's president, said Azerbaijan didn't require economic incentives to make an agreement. "We have won the war, and we wanted to win the peace," Hajiyev said.

In a video address played at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for Firebird, Huang described the project as the first step in an effort to "connect this region to the global AI economy" and said it would be "a magnet, an opportunity to attract companies around the world to build and run their AI here."

In February, Vice President JD Vance visited Armenia to tout the deal and told Pashinyan, the Armenian prime minister, that "the United States was proud to issue a number of export licenses for the sale of high-powered Nvidia chips." The move would mean "new markets for American workers and for American businesses, but it also means greater prosperity for the people of Armenia," Vance said.

In a two-page memo produced by U.S. Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff's team, dated June of 2025, the Americans outlined a plan to deepen Armenia's economic relationship with the U.S. and bolster the country's tech industry, including giving export licenses for the Firebird chips, as part of the peace deal.

The U.S. proposed building a corridor featuring rail lines, pipelines and roads connecting Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, its landlocked exclave that sits between Armenia and Turkey whose population is more than 99% Azerbaijani. Construction on that project-known as the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity-is set to begin in early 2027.

Rev Lebaredian, a senior Nvidia executive who is of Armenian descent, helped forge ties between the company and Prime Minister Pashinyan. He said the cooperation on AI and the trade corridor could help create an economic interdependence between Armenia, Azerbaijan and other countries in the region that could lead to a durable peace.

"For this administration, chip diplomacy is front and center," Lebaredian said in an interview. "Our presence in Armenia and our investment in it is a big factor in creating the conditions by which peace can unfold."

American diplomats, including then-U.S. Ambassador to Armenia Kristina Kvien, promoted the idea of using access to technology as a carrot to reach a deal over the summer, meeting with Commerce Department officials to ask them to authorize the sale of Nvidia's most advanced chips to Armenia, which had previously not been approved to receive them, according to Kvien and others directly involved in the negotiations.  "Firebird is the most tangible thing that Prime Minister Pashinyan can point to and say, 'Peace delivered this,'" said Sen. Steve Daines, a Republican of Montana, who met with Pashinyan in Armenia in May of last year alongside the White House team negotiating the deal. "Getting the chips was a crucial political win."

Firebird had already applied for an export license for around 6,000 GPUs, or graphics processing units, a common type of AI chips, but it wasn't until after the preliminary peace agreement was reached last August that U.S. officials delivered on their promise to approve tens of thousands more of Nvidia's leading-edge processors, known as GB300s.

"You needed peace conditions," said Razmig Hovaghimian, the Armenian-American co-founder and CEO of Firebird. "The technology stack needs to be safe and secure in order to attract international customers."

The U.S. ended up striking bilateral economic cooperation deals with both Armenia and Azerbaijan as a way of offering "sweeteners" to the peace negotiations, said Kvien, the former ambassador.  "The Nvidia piece of it was a very important piece of the puzzle," Kvien said.
